# Harvest: Google PAIR People + AI Guidebook (third edition, "Generative AI Edition", updated April 2025)

Source: https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/ - harvested from the live site on 2026-08-01.

Scope: 6 chapters / 20 section pages, the chapter overview callouts, the home page, and the Principles & Patterns page (`/guidebook/patterns`).

Structural note: PAIR publishes **5 named Principles** and **23 named Patterns**. Neither is numbered - they are addressed by name and grouped on-site under eight questions, not by index. There is no numbered pattern scheme anywhere in the live Guidebook.

Claims are verbatim or trimmed-verbatim from the page text. Source typos are preserved as-is.

| 10 |  PRINCIPLE - User Autonomy: "Design for the appropriate level of user autonomy" - "AI-supported workflows should be designed for the appropriate level of user autonomy, that consider different user tasks, expertise, and the overall effort required to steer the AI system." | Principles | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/patterns |
| 11 |  User Autonomy rationale: "People also prefer to remain in control of which tasks tools should execute, how, and to what end. Knowing when a user is willing to delegate a task to an AI, how users can control the AI, and when to leave control with the user entirely is key for building helpful AI products." | Principles | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/patterns |
| 12 |  PRINCIPLE - Data & Model Alignment: "Align AI with real-world behaviors" - "People engage differently with AI systems based on their context. Align datasets and models to people's interactions with AI systems in real world contexts." | Principles | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/patterns |
| 13 |  Data & Model Alignment rationale: "As your AI products scales, it may be utilized for unexpected tasks, socio-technical contexts, or knowledge domains. Natural and intuitive interactions with AI systems can differ in surprising ways from standard benchmarks, training or tuning data. It's essential to align your user journeys, data collection and model evaluation efforts with AI interactions that might occur in real-world contexts, as early as possible." | Principles | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/patterns |
| 14 |  PRINCIPLE - Evolving Safety: "Treat safety as an evolving endeavor" - "AI products should have a multifaceted safety strategy that evolves with technology and people. Account for varying degrees of risk and ensure people's safety, now and in the future." | Principles | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/patterns |
| 15 |  Evolving Safety rationale: "Changes in user context and complexity can introduce new or exacerbate existing risks, beyond the scope of your AI product. Proactively develop safeguards for different risk levels in your product's user experience and AI models. Be prepared to adapt and modify safety strategies to respond to evolving trends and behaviors." | Principles | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/patterns |
| 16 |  PRINCIPLE - Adapt with Feedback: "Adapt your AI system with feedback from people, during individual interactions and over time." | Principles | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/patterns |
| 17 |  Adapt with Feedback rationale: "Human-AI interactions are a bidirectional feedback loop. AI learns from users to personalize their experiences, and users adapt their behaviors and workflows in response to AI outcomes. Set up feedback mechanisms that can be used to interpret AI outcomes, and account for changes introduced by AI." | Principles | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/patterns |
| 18 |  PRINCIPLE - Helpful AI: "Create helpful AI experiences that enhance aspects of work & play that people enjoy and inspire creativity." | Principles | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/patterns |
| 19 |  Helpful AI rationale: "AI can amplify human expertise, but the efficiency gains aren't always assured, cheaper, or enjoyable. People have certain expectations of benefit and performance that AI should deliver." | Principles | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/patterns |
| 20 |  "Our product principles provide directional guidance while highlight opportunities and challenges that teams experience when building experiences with AI. Illustrated with hypothetical applications. Last updated May 24, 2024." | Principles | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/ |

| 216 |  If your team does not have a product yet, understand how current AI solutions may be used and what their shortcomings are. | User Needs + Defining Success > Identify user needs and AI strengths | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/identify-user-needs-and-ai-strengths/ |
| 217 |  To get an understanding of how people might use a product like yours, you can also prototype your idea in a tool like Google AI Studio and see how people feel about the results. | User Needs + Defining Success > Identify user needs and AI strengths | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/identify-user-needs-and-ai-strengths/ |

| 221 |  Use this understanding to inform decisions about integrating AI into your product. | User Needs + Defining Success > Identify user needs and AI strengths | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/identify-user-needs-and-ai-strengths/ |

| 230 |  However, these approaches are not mutually exclusive. Sometimes the best solutions feature a combination of both. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 231 |  Knowing when to automate, augment, or leave control with the user is key for building helpful AI products. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 232 |  Another consideration is how automation complacency and automation bias can create challenges for people using your product. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 233 |  It's important to design with the possibility of automation complacency and bias from the start. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 234 |  Consider what would happen if people experienced either automation complacency or automation bias in your AI product. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 235 |  The more consequential the outcome, the more human oversight should be required. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 236 |  Automation occurs when a machine, software, or function performs a task with minimal to no user intervention. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 237 |  Augmentation occurs when a machine, software, or function amplifies the user's own capabilities to discover new insights and efficiencies collaboratively. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 238 |  Automation complacency occurs when people don't monitor an automated process they believe to be reliable or fail to pay sufficient attention to its output as much as they should. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 239 |  This can lead to a directly observable, negative effect on product performance. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 240 |  Automation bias describes a tendency to place too much trust in a support mechanism, especially when there are errors of omission (e.g., GPS doesn't say to turn left, but you should have) or commission (e.g., GPS tells you to turn left when you shouldn't have). | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 241 |  People are excited about AI, but don't always understand AI. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 242 |  When new technologies, like generative AI, are introduced to the public, it takes time for people to form their understanding of the technology. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 243 |  Their expectations are built on existing systems and product experiences. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 244 |  People may not fully understand generative AI's capabilities and limitations, how their data is being used to improve models, or how best to craft the right input for the results they need. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 245 |  Your product's capacity to support people as they explore your AI system's capabilities and limitations will be critical to its success. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 246 |  When choosing between automation, augmentation, or a mix of the two, consider: What are users trying to do? | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 247 |  When choosing between automation, augmentation, or a mix of the two, consider: What tasks do they need to execute? | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 248 |  When choosing between automation, augmentation, or a mix of the two, consider: Do they understand how your AI product works? | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 249 |  When choosing between automation, augmentation, or a mix of the two, consider: How much do they know about what they're trying to do? | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 250 |  If they were training a coworker for a similar role, what would be the most important tasks they would teach first? | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 251 |  If they had a human assistant to work with on a task, what duties would be delegated? | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 252 |  Automation often makes sense when it allows people to improve their productivity, avoid repetitive tasks, or when the time, money, or effort necessary to complete a task isn't worth it to them to spend. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 253 |  Sometimes, people are happy to delegate these tasks to AI when they don't require oversight or they can be done just as well by someone (or something) else. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |

Do people perceive that performance is increased by some measure? | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |

| 258 |  Successful automation is often measured by improved human safety: Does the automation reduce the risk to the human operator and improve the outcomes of their decisions? | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |

| 261 |  While students or professionals may automate tasks related to their original work, any automation that violates a policy or law (e.g., cheating on homework, a person claiming credit for an automated translation or computer code) should not be encouraged. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 262 |  If the outcomes of acceptable automated tasks are irreversible or high-risk, people should be able to apply their judgment and explicitly decide if an automation should occur. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 263 |  Consider automation for challenging tasks that exceed a person's knowledge, expertise, or skill level. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 264 |  In this scenario, automation should simplify the experience such that people can easily evaluate the AI output and make decisions. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |

| 266 |  In this scenario, people should be able to customize or define how much assistance they require from the automation. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |

| 268 |  In this scenario, people operating the automation should be informed of the system's status and be able to delegate or take control. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 269 |  Sometimes people prefer to avoid tasks requiring substantial work in proportion to the value of results, especially when they need to perform the task frequently. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 270 |  Consider automation for low value tasks that require more effort than the value offered (e.g., checking a document for small typos manually instead of using spell-check). | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 271 |  Consider automation for tedious tasks that detract from the end goal. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 272 |  Tasks that can be broken down into sequential steps, which when followed exactly, have very little chance of error are usually better candidates for automating. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |

| 274 |  Consider automation for low-risk tasks that have very little chance of error when proper steps are followed (e.g., suggesting responses to a message a user has received). | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |
| 275 |  In this scenario, there should always be an option for human oversight — and intervention if necessary. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |

| 278 |  When building AI-powered products, it's tempting to assume that the best thing you can do for your users is automate tasks they currently do manually. | User Needs + Defining Success > Balance automation and augmentation | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/balance-automation-and-augmentation/ |

| 478 |  Design Policies serve user needs in measurable ways. | User Needs + Defining Success > Define interaction design policies | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/define-interaction-design-policies/ |

However, this isn't the best approach. | User Needs + Defining Success > Define interaction design policies | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/define-interaction-design-policies/ |
| 485 |  When you apply a simple, narrow, and immediate design policy to broad audiences over time, there can be unintended negative effects. | User Needs + Defining Success > Define interaction design policies | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/define-interaction-design-policies/ |
| 486 |  It's important to evaluate your design policy at the critical moment, but also as a whole. | User Needs + Defining Success > Define interaction design policies | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/define-interaction-design-policies/ |
| 487 |  Your design policy should be something that you can evaluate and verify at many points in the product life cycle; and should reasonably translate into a set of quantitative and qualitative measures. | User Needs + Defining Success > Define interaction design policies | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/define-interaction-design-policies/ |
| 488 |  Ideally, these should be centered around critical moments in the product experience. | User Needs + Defining Success > Define interaction design policies | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/define-interaction-design-policies/ |
| 489 |  Decide on quantitative metrics that meaningfully capture user satisfaction, task success, and model performance. | User Needs + Defining Success > Define interaction design policies | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/define-interaction-design-policies/ |
| 490 |  Define a set of qualitative criteria that can capture model outcomes that drive product success, and those that can create risk. | User Needs + Defining Success > Define interaction design policies | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/define-interaction-design-policies/ |
| 491 |  In each of these moments, there are likely tricky conditions where the people who use your system bump up against your design policies. | User Needs + Defining Success > Define interaction design policies | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/define-interaction-design-policies/ |
| 492 |  Just relying on technical measures can create blind spots, so it's important to conduct human-in-the-loop evaluations and user research. | User Needs + Defining Success > Define interaction design policies | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/define-interaction-design-policies/ |
| 493 |  Consider using mixed-methods assessments to evaluate how your model performs under these conditions. | User Needs + Defining Success > Define interaction design policies | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/define-interaction-design-policies/ |
| 494 |  You can test your design policies through lightweight prototypes with users even before your model is ready. | User Needs + Defining Success > Define interaction design policies | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/define-interaction-design-policies/ |

| 501 |  Consider: Quantitative analogs to ground subjective human preferences. | User Needs + Defining Success > Define interaction design policies | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/define-interaction-design-policies/ |

| 510 |  Example policy: Don't introduce any gender-specific stereotypes or offensive content; outputs should not contain or propagate any stereotypes or introduce caricatures pertaining to the gender(s) indicated in the input. | User Needs + Defining Success > Define interaction design policies | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/define-interaction-design-policies/ |

| 514 |  Mixed-method assessments can help complex scenarios. | User Needs + Defining Success > Define interaction design policies | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/define-interaction-design-policies/ |

| 521 |  Past technological interventions can teach us which signals indicate future change. | User Needs + Defining Success > Prepare for potential pitfalls | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/prepare-for-potential-pitfalls/ |

| 523 |  And even if it were, the expectations and perceptions of the individuals and groups who use it, and the world we live in are constantly shifting. | User Needs + Defining Success > Prepare for potential pitfalls | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/prepare-for-potential-pitfalls/ |
| 524 |  Acknowledge that errors can seep through the user experience, and empower your team to imagine the potential pitfalls of incorporating AI into your product and address second-order effects. | User Needs + Defining Success > Prepare for potential pitfalls | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/prepare-for-potential-pitfalls/ |

| 527 |  Second-order consequence example: With a better understanding of individual student needs, teachers start to personalize assignments to students and evaluate students on improvements over multiple drafts and assignments. | User Needs + Defining Success > Prepare for potential pitfalls | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/prepare-for-potential-pitfalls/ |
| 528 |  Second-order effects are the consequences of the consequences of a certain action. | User Needs + Defining Success > Prepare for potential pitfalls | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/prepare-for-potential-pitfalls/ |
| 529 |  Effects that are second-order or more are difficult to predict with absolute certainty, but it's possible to anticipate trends or conditions that can send the desired impact of your product off course. | User Needs + Defining Success > Prepare for potential pitfalls | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/prepare-for-potential-pitfalls/ |

| 532 |  Identifying potential pitfalls can be useful for proactive mitigations: Anticipating potential failures, risks, and harms that might be associated with your product to proactively plan mitigations. | User Needs + Defining Success > Prepare for potential pitfalls | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/prepare-for-potential-pitfalls/ |

| 548 |  Start by bringing together individuals with a variety of expertise and lived experience. | User Needs + Defining Success > Prepare for potential pitfalls | https://pair.withgoogle.com/guidebook/chapters/user-needs-and-defining-success/prepare-for-potential-pitfalls/ |

## Coverage notes

- **PAIR has no numbered patterns.** Confirmed. It publishes 5 named **Principles** (User Autonomy, Data & Model Alignment, Evolving Safety, Adapt with Feedback, Helpful AI) and 23 named **Patterns**, grouped on-site under eight questions ("How do I get started with human-centered AI?", "When and how should I use AI in my product?", "How do I explain my AI system to users?", "How do I help users build and calibrate trust in my product?", "How do I support users when something goes wrong?", "How do I responsibly build my dataset?", "How do I onboard users to new AI features?", "What's the right balance of user control and automation?"). No index numbers exist anywhere in the live Guidebook.
- **The Guidebook is fully client-rendered.** A plain HTTP GET of any route returns the same 205,486-byte JS shell with zero prose. Content was obtained two independent ways and cross-checked: (1) rendering each route in a browser and traversing the shadow DOM; (2) extracting the content template literals embedded in `assets/main-SMD7SNZ6.js`. All 20 section pages' first headings matched 1:1 between the two methods, so the mapping from extracted text to URL is verified, not assumed.
- **Source typos preserved.** e.g. "We don't want {people or users} to intentionally or intentionally use our product's AI" (User Needs > Define interaction design policies) and "THow people use your product..." (Mental Models > Identify existing mental models) appear as printed.
- **Deliberately excluded from the rows:** the Glossary (~100 term definitions, fetched but reference material rather than guidance), Case Studies, Workshops, the downloadable worksheet PDFs, and the archived v2 Guidebook.
